Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette: Leena, a 48-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married tutor, has been seeking help for symptoms that have significantly disrupted her daily life. Her experience of severe physical abuse at the hands of her romantic partner has left deep emotional scars. Leena vividly recalls the night when everything changed; she was in her home, going about her usual evening routine, when her partner’s anger erupted into a violent outburst. The intensity and unpredictability of that moment have instilled a sense of permanent damage within her. Leena’s fears and negative appraisals—such as feeling like an outsider and believing that you can never truly know who will harm you—have made it difficult for her to process the fragmented pieces of the traumatic event. Whenever she tries to recall the incident, it feels like flipping through a series of photographic snapshots that don’t quite align with one another. This disconnection has led Leena to experience intense terror each time she attempts to revisit those memories. She is certain that she has been permanently changed for the worse, and this conviction makes it even harder for her to integrate the fragmented pieces into a coherent narrative. The memory of the event has become intertwined with her heightened sense of threat, as she now constantly scans her surroundings for signs of danger. Leena’s hypervigilance is not limited to just noticing potential weapons; she also feels that her body reacts to perceived threats before her mind can fully process them. This constant state of alertness reinforces her negative beliefs and keeps her in a heightened state of fear. As a tutor, Leena often has to navigate the school environment, which has become increasingly challenging due to her hypervigilance towards people she perceives as potentially dangerous. She spends much time checking mirrors for any signs of danger, mirroring her broader pattern of scanning environments for threats. This behavior, while intended to keep her safe, has led to a significant decrease in her sense of security and trust. The constant vigilance and checking behaviors have also created a cycle where Leena feels increasingly threatened by the slightest disturbances in her environment. Her fear that any object could be turned into a weapon has made it difficult for her to engage fully with her surroundings without feeling a persistent sense of danger. This hypervigilance has extended beyond her personal life, affecting her interactions at work and in social settings. Leena’s experiences have led her to feel like an outsider, further exacerbating her negative appraisals about herself and the world around her. Her belief that she is permanently damaged for the worse makes it hard for her to imagine a future where these traumatic memories no longer dominate her thoughts. The combination of fragmented memories, hypervigilance, and deeply ingrained fears has created an overwhelming sense of disconnection from both her past and present. What finally brought Leena to seek help was the realization that her symptoms were interfering with her ability to continue tutoring effectively and maintain meaningful relationships with her loved ones. She is most afraid of never feeling safe again and hopes that therapy can provide her with tools to manage these overwhelming fears and begin rebuilding a sense of security in her life.
